overview: “Hindu states” is a changing atlas label for parts of India between 700 and 1000, not one kingdom. Its outlines jump from the northeast to western and peninsular regions, then shrink to a tiny northern fragment. These examples belong to distinct communities and dynasties, not a uniform religious population.

periods.title: Northeastern regional context
periods.summary: Ambari’s medieval occupation began around the seventh century and continued beyond this snapshot.

periods.title: Western and eastern peninsular contexts
periods.summary: Vengi’s Eastern Chalukyas were a distinct dynasty, not rulers of every area under this label.

periods.title: Continuing kingdoms beyond a shrinking outline
periods.summary: Copper grants of Amma I and Amma II document Vengi institutions despite the map’s tiny surviving northern patch.

items.text: The 700 outline covers parts of Bengal and Assam. In 800 the label instead covers disconnected western and eastern peninsular areas; by 900 it is a small fragment in northern Uttar Pradesh. Abhaneri, discussed here for regional comparison, falls outside the sampled outlines. None of these boundaries establishes a shared religion or government.

Vengi inscriptions describe enemies, relatives and rival claimants rather than a united religious bloc. Amma I’s Ederu charter praises him for overcoming hostile kinsmen and winning his father’s troops. These are a court’s claims about a particular succession struggle; the neighbouring Rashtrakutas and other dynasties require their own histories.

Ambari, in present-day Guwahati, was rediscovered during foundation digging for a Reserve Bank building in 1969. ASI distinguishes an occupation phase from roughly the seventh to twelfth centuries. A modern construction project opened a window onto a much older settlement; its later remains must be separated from that medieval phase.

Ambari also yielded Chinese celadon dated to the tenth to twelfth centuries. Some therefore belongs after this map window. Such pottery points to connections beyond the Brahmaputra valley, although a traded bowl alone cannot identify who carried it or who ate from it.

At Tezpur, a boulder beside the Brahmaputra carries a decree of Harjjaravarman dated 829 to 830. ASI describes a warning to fishermen about crossing a marked fishing area. River resources required rules as well as boats. This belongs to later Kamarupa history, after the atlas label has shifted away from Assam.

Scholars also read references to boatmen in state service in the Tezpur inscription. River work linked food gathering, transport and royal administration. Fishing communities were participants in the region’s economy, not just background figures in stories about kings. The article’s descriptions of modern Majuli life cannot simply be assigned to the ninth century.

Chand Baori at Abhaneri descends approximately 19.5 metres, with repeated flights of steps on three sides. Official accounts place its early construction around the eighth or ninth century. The changing water level could be approached down the staircase: getting water involved a rather longer walk than turning a tap.

Rajasthan Tourism describes Chand Baori as both a water-conserving structure and a gathering place offering relief from the heat. Water infrastructure could create social space. Its spectacular surviving galleries belong to a monument with a building history, so every visible feature should not be dated to the first construction campaign.

In Vengi, the museum history credits Vijayaditya II, an early ninth-century ruler, with feeding houses, shelters offering drinking water to travellers, and irrigation tanks. These activities supported movement and cultivation as well as religious patronage. A water station was a practical kindness on a hot journey.

sections.title: Families, fields and learning in Vengi

items.text: The Cevuru charter of Amma I, from the early tenth century, links a favour to the soldier Vemaraja with Prince Vijayaditya’s first rice-feeding ceremony. A royal child’s milestone became an occasion for public generosity. This is one documented court celebration, not a rule for every family.

The same charter locates fields using a marshy pool, a stream, neighbouring land and the king’s field. Telugu landscape words appear inside its formal Sanskrit framework. A legal document needed landmarks people could recognize: grand royal titles did not replace knowing which stream bordered the field.

A grant of Vijayaditya II in Pishtapura district names a recipient’s father and grandfather and praises the family’s Vedic learning. Land patronage supported specialist scholarship across generations. This is evidence for a learned Brahman family, rather than a census of children attending school.

That grant was made at Trikotishvara during a lunar eclipse and confirmed by pouring water. It then lists neighbouring villages to define the property. Ceremony and practical geography belonged together: the water marked a formal gift, while the boundaries specified what was actually being given.

Amma I’s Ederu charter awarded Gonturu and twelve hamlets to a military retainer, with a tax exemption. Such grants show how rulers rewarded service through local resources. The document publicly addressed householders in the district, reminding us that a royal gift affected people already living and working there.

The Ederu charter praises Chalukya Bhima I for supporting distressed and helpless people alongside dancers and singers. It presents generosity as an attribute of good kingship. The wording records a royal ideal and a claim of patronage; it does not identify a hospital or establish the reach of medical care.

sections.title: Crafts, different faiths and surviving words

items.text: Copper charters were substantial handmade objects. An Indian Museum set from Chandavallu consists of three plates, a ring and an inscribed seal associated with Vijayaditya II. The plates measure only about fourteen by five centimetres. Important royal information could be packed into a small, durable metal bundle.

A later Vengi grant, from Amma II’s reign in the mid-tenth century, gave land to two Jain temples at Vijayavatika, now Vijayawada. It is a useful check on the atlas shorthand. A dynasty associated with Hindu royal language could also support Jain institutions; religious life was not neatly contained by a map colour.

One authentic word is “स्वस्ति” (svasti), “Greetings,” opening Amma I’s Cevuru charter. The Sanskrit appears here in modern Devanagari, not the original southern letterforms. The charter also uses Telugu “koḍu,” “stream,” shown in scholarly Roman transcription. Both belong to this early tenth-century Vengi document, not a language shared by everyone under the atlas label.

The Cevuru plates were found around 1928 when Polavarapu Ankayya cleared debris from a collapsed mud house. Chhabra later borrowed them for study. An ordinary repair or clearing job could recover a royal document that had long outlived its original owners.

ending.text: The atlas endpoint of 1000 is not a common fall date. Vengi’s struggles continued, including Chola-backed intervention around 1000, while regional communities and religious institutions endured. This shifting umbrella ends as a map label; the named kingdoms have separate political histories.
